My name is Austin Dow-Smith, and I am an MSSM alumnus from the class of 2012. I am writing to emphasize the profound impact that MSSM has on Maine's students.
MSSM sparked my interest in STEM through its summer camps in middle school and provided a rigorous academic environment from 2009 to 2012. The challenge of catching up with peers honed my problem-solving skills and instilled perseverance--tools that have been invaluable throughout my education and career.
Equally important, MSSM fostered a close-knit community where lasting friendships and support networks were built--benefits that extend into college and professional life. 10040032:
To the members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee,

My name is Autumn Baldwin, and I am writing to provide you with my written

testimony for your consideration on two bills impacting The Maine School of Science

and Mathematics. The bills LD787 and LD1011 would be of great benefit to not only

MSSM, but also to the State of Maine as a whole. I will give you just one small

example of how passing both of these bills can change the lives of students across this

state.

My son, Nikolias Theriault, is a senior at The Maine School of Science and

Mathematics. This school has changed the course of Niko's life. Nikolias was

identified as a gift student in Kindergarten. During the two years he attended

Fiddlehead Charter School in Gray, Niko began to dream of attending MSSM.

Passionate about all things science, technology, engineering, and math - he was drawn

to the challenge this school provided in the fields he was the most interested in. From

fourth grade on, Niko focused on doing whatever it took to attend this school. I

supported him in every way that I could - all while being fearful that although it was

his dream, and the tuition would be covered as Maine residents, without financial

assistance - how hard we worked would not have mattered.

I am a seventh year educator in this state, and without financial assistance, I

would not have been able to afford to pay for Nikolias' room and board. His father

was out of his life for many years, addicted to drugs and in and out of jail. I did not

receive any child support and as a single mother with two children, on a teacher's

salary - Niko attending MSSM seemed unattainable. I told Niko I would do

everything I could to help him attend, but it truly did boil down to financial aid. He

never complained, and we waited so eagerly and patiently together for the day we

received his package information.

I will never forget the day that we received his financial aid package. His

acceptance was the first hurdle that we felt we were in control of. This was not - and

his attendance and dream clung to this. Through financial aid assistance, our family

contribution that first year for Niko to attend brought the cost to us from $10,000 to

$660. I remember that day, that feeling and my emotion as I could finally tell my son

that his dream had truly come true. He was going to attend The Maine School of

Science and Mathematics. Niko has received financial aid every year that he has been

there, with the awards being a little higher each year. I do not have adequate words to

fully express what the financial aid has meant to our family. Without it, he would not

be where he is today.

The Maine School of Science and Mathematics has changed the course of my

son's life. He has been challenged academically unlike any public school he has been

to. Prior to his attendance at MSSM, Niko was often bored and disengaged in the

classroom. Having a gifted son is the reason I went back later in life to become a

teacher myself. Throughout his time at MSSM, he was able to pick challenging

courses with professors that held doctorate degrees in their fields. The academic rigor

has given Niko an opportunity to excel and be challenged, and has well prepared him

for his college journey ahead. He has been able to play sports and is surrounded by a

community of like-minded children, and people. This school is not just strong

academically, although that cannot be understated. This is a school that genuinely

and wholeheartedly cares about every student that attends, helping them to become

the best version of themselves academically, socially, emotionally and physically.

As a mother of a student at this school, I have been continually impressed by

every aspect of what makes this school so wonderful. This school focuses on building

a small community that cares about each other, which is so critical as so many of

these students are hundreds of miles away from their own families. I truly feel that my

son is at a school surrounded by people that love and admire him as much as I do. My

son has been able to shine, show who he truly is and continually be celebrated for it.

This school does so much with so little - and ensures that each student that is a

perfect fit for MSSM, is able to attend regardless of ability to pay.

As you can see, MSSM is a gift to the state of Maine and to each student that

attends. LD787 proposes to increase the funding to MSSM by $400,000 for general

operations and $250,000 for student financial aid. These are both critical increases to

ensure that MSSM is able to continue helping students achieve their dreams, and

continue to grow their community of learners while maintaining a strong school. The

increase to their financial aid is so critical in these challenging financial times. There

are many students, like Niko, who are unfortunately unable to attend without this. An

increase in financial aid of $250,000 a year means at minimum 20 more students per

year can attend with nearly a free room and board, and when considering partial aid

grants, it increases even more.

I ask that you please consider my son's journey and story when making the

decision to pass these critical bills. MSSM is a gift to the students who attend, the

families who support it and we are so lucky that Maine has this educational

opportunity. I ask that you please pass both of these bills, and any in the future that allow The Maine School of Science and Mathematics to continue to grow as a powerful educational institution. This is not just another high school, it is a true educational experience for gifted students. Niko's story is just one - and watching him graduate this May from this school will be a dream come true for both of us. Lastly, I would like to thank Sen. Nicole Grohoski of Hancock, and Sen. Sue Bernard of Aroostook respectfully for sponsoring this bill and seeing the true gift that this school is to the state of Maine.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Autumn Baldwin

10039534:
Dear Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Marian Reagan and I am the current elected Chair of the appointed Board of Trustees of the Maine School of Science and Mathematics. I am also a parent of an MSSM graduate and a resident of Kennebunkport, ME. I was appointed to the MSSM Board by the Governor and confirmed by the Legislature in 2018 and am in my second year serving as Chair.
As the appointed fiduciaries of MSSM, the Board of Trustees are responsible for ensuring both the viability of MSSM and that public funds are used appropriately and efficiently. This is not a responsibility we take lightly we work closely with the School's administration to develop a balanced budget each year, receive and review regular performance reports from the School's administration, and conduct an independent audit of the School's finances and internal controls each year.
During my time on the Board, MSSM has received flat funding for its operations. Even through a period of normal inflation, this would be a significant challenge for any organization. Given the high inflation rates that we have seen in recent years, the impact of flat funding has been crippling to MSSM's ability to deliver on its mission. I am almost embarrassed to represent the State of Maine in asking the School's administration to find more operational savings. In almost every year I have been on the Board, the administration has presented the elimination of a position. I have watched the School eliminate 5 FTEs in just the past two years - good jobs for Mainers and jobs that are important to serving the students of Maine. I have seen the School continue to shrink its discretionary spending (things outside of rent, utilities, food service) - for next year the School committed to finding 10% or more in savings in this area - cuts to things like academic supplies, student activities, athletics, and other areas that are important to serving the students Maine committed to serving when MSSM was established 30 years ago. At the same time, the School increased its financial aid budget to 10% of its entire appropriation.
We have heard that some of our recent flat funding has been because we didn't follow the appropriate process with the Department of Education. The Board charged the executive director with ensuring we do this and, in June 2024, MSSM submitted a budget proposal for the next biennial to the Department of Education as requested. We suggested modest increases of $250,000 for the 2025-26 year and $116,000 for the 2026-27 year. These increases did not address years of flat-funding, did not provide for investment in exciting initiatives to better serve our students, and were accompanied by increased expectations on the School increasing its other revenue sources. Despite following the process and the modest increases, the School was informed that the DOE would not include any additional funding for the next biennial.
Even with this funding travesty, I remain impressed with the School's delivery on its mission. This year, the School has retained 100% of its students to date - a significant accomplishment unmatched in its history that represents the efforts to address student well being and mental health. The School has seen the highest number of inquiries and applicants in the last five years, and we are projecting reversing several years of enrollment declines next year. The School has been developing partnerships to expand its impact beyond just the students living on campus. The School's administration has worked with the Board to look forward and we are in the midst of a comprehensive and exciting strategic planning process. And, even while accomplishing all of this, the School's administration again cut some positions, found more savings, and sacrificed some more programming in an effort to present a balanced budget for tomorrow.
It is time to reverse this blatant disregard for this important Maine institution. It is time to own the decision that Maine made 30 years ago when it established a STEM magnet school and one of only a small number of

public boarding schools in the country. It is time to treat Maine's students better and recognize that there are two sides of the special needs continuum and that MSSM is an efficient and effective way to serve the high end of that continuum that has demonstrated success. It is time to invest in educational success - like we continue to see at MSSM.
Thank you for considering LD787 and I encourage you to move this important bill forward with your highest recommendation.
10040154:
Miles Sweet Scarborough LD 787
I write in support of LD 787 and LD 1011 for the Maine School of Science and Mathematics in Limestone.
It's one of the places I call home. I'm originally from Central Maine's rural Kennebec Valley, and I was the first student from outside of Aroostook County to visit what would become MSSM more than 30 years ago. At the end of the Cold War, when the bases at Loring and Brunswick closed, all levels of government agreed to invest in an experiment in the pursuit of excellence. The Legislature's school. A place where students from all 16 counties could live together, learn how to collaborate on big projects, and compete in an increasingly globalized and interconnected world. It's a place I came back to as a science camp teacher in the summer between becoming the first person in my family to graduate from college and starting my doctorate in chemistry at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar.
On the 25th anniversary of my graduation from MSSM, I was invited back to give the commencement address. Students asked me what had changed. The food is better, the dorms more comfortable, and the technology is beyond anything we might have imagined in the 1990s. But what has remained the same for decades is a commitment to community, the highest standards of learning results, and a grateful appreciation to the people of Maine for their Legislature's school. Parents told me they knew it was a safe place where their children could also find a home, challenge themselves, and unlock their potential. You make that possible.
Ensuring success for generations to come is one of the reasons I moved back to Maine and joined the Board of Directors for the MSSM Foundation, the booster club that helps coordinate fans of the school - mostly family, alums, faculty and staff - who donate money, goods, and time to help enhance that margin of excellence. commitment to MSSM that the Maine State Legislature has provided.
Fast forward to 2025: Ongoing funding declines have made it harder to keep excellent faculty and
staff, and essential positions have been cut. Room and board is $10,850, and, while financial aid is available, sticker shock keeps a lot of families from applying. I am saddened and embarrassed that the State has allowed the school to reach the level of hardship it now faces. However, I am also
hopeful that this committee and the l32nd Legislature will build on the investment it made in the
131st Legislature and take further action to save the school.
In 2020, this committee asked the school to see what it could do to help itself financially, which
resulted in the establishment of an ad hoc "Business Planning Committee" of the MSSM Board.` At
the end of 2020, this committee shared its findings with the Board and the Department of
Education.' The committee compared the MS SM funding structure to six states' science and math
public residential magnet schools. Here are a few slides of particular interest:
In 2020, Maine ranked lowest for the state share of the school budget at 68%, with Mississippi the
second lowest at 75% and North Carolina and Arkansas at 100% (Slide 40).
1
The Business Planning Committee Chaiter is available here: bit.ly/MSSM-business-plan-charter 2 The Committee's presentation can be viewed here: bit.|y/MSSM-presentation
2

Maine also charged families significantly more for room and board, which is now up to $10,850 (Slide 41). As you can see, most states charge nominal amounts, including $0 in North Carolina.
The long and short of the Business Plamiing Committee effort is this - MSSM is an outlier when it
comes to its school funding model. If we want it to stay in the same location and offer the excellent education it is known for - which by all accounts continues despite the dwindling funding -- then the
State needs to step up with resources.
I attended MSSM in my junior and senior years of high school, seeking a rigorous education in math
and science, at a price my family could afford (room and board was less� expensive back then). I found the curricular options and rigor to be beyond my imagination. I worked harder than I had ever
needed to before and gained real knowledge and a new confidence in myself and what I could
achieve.
There's more to life at MSSM than just academics. For me, this was the first time I was surrounded
by a group of students who I really connected with. No one made fun of me for wanting to dig
deeper into a tough topic; instead, they'd often join in. I competed in sports and played music in the
band at the University of Maine at Presque Isle. As members of the Key Club, my friends and I were
reading mentors to young students in nearby schools. I was an officer in the student senate and set up the school's first recycling program. I mention all of this to show the diversity of experiences one
student can have at MSSM -- well beyond just the excellent academic opportunities.
When I graduated from MSSM, I left with the skills to learn tough subjects and a solid academic base that made my transition to college seamless. I made lifelong friends, who are contributing to
this state and country in incredible ways. I cannot say where I would be today without having
3

attended MSSM, but I am certain that it was an opportunity that changed my life significantly and
positively.
I am grateful that the State had the vision to create such an institution of excellence. I know that it
was life-changing for so many of my peers who came from small, rural schools that lacked large
enough student bodies to suppoit high-level courses available at MS SM. Now in its 30th year, the
school needs our financial support to continue to help Maine students reach their full potential. Investing in these students and the school is an investment in our state's future.
Thank you for your time and consideration of my testimony. I would be happy to answer any
questions.

Paul Stancioff Camden LD 787
I have been on the board of trustees of the Maine School of Science and Mathematics since September of 2022. As such I have learned what a gem this institution is. As a retired educator, I have been extremely impressed with the quality and dedication of the faculty and staff.
MSSM has been essentially flat funded for the last 8 years. With inflation, this is equivalent to a 30% decrease in real money. The administration has had to make difficult and strategic decisions to reduce staff over several years. At this point there is virtually no room for further cuts.
The other part of this bill simply changes the residency requirement to no longer require a six-month residency before enrolling at MMSM with the in-state benefits. This seems obvious to me. If someone moves from out of state to any other school district in Maine, they do not have a six month wait to send their children to school.
MSSM plays an important role in our state's education system. It gives the opportunity for students to pursue interests that would be unavailable at many of the local high schools in Maine. It also gives opportunity for families for whom other options (such as a private school) would be far out of reach.
187514:
Good afternoon Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and the members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. My name is Rob Constantine and I am the current Executive Director of the Maine School
of Science and Mathematics. l am happy to be here today to voice my support for LD787 and to answer any questions any members of the Committee may have regarding the School's annual report submitted at the
start of the session or how things are going this year.
First, I urge you to support changing the residency language of our statute as laid out in both LD787 and LD1011. While the language is slightly different, the change to statute in both of these bills ensures that public
funds appropriated for MSSM truly benefit Maine families. The way our founding statute currently reads,
students must reside in the state for 6 months prior to application in order to be eligible for free in-state tuition.
When l meet with employers, l often hear that MSSM is an important recruiting tool when they bring employees
into Maine to fill positions in their Maine-based businesses. In order to continue to serve in this way, it is
important that qualified students who relocate to Maine with their families are eligible for in-state free tuition regardless of when they move here - like they would be at any other public school in Maine. At the same time, conditioning residency determination to the time of application allows students who move out of the state to
continue to qualify for in-state tuition. By moving to an annual determination linked to the start of the School
year, you would eliminate this potential loophole.
l also urge you to consider appropriating the additional funds in LD787 for MSSM. l have shared before that
MSSM has received a static appropriation for several years - this next biennial will be our 9th and 10th years
with the same amount. lf you've been to the grocery store, or filled your heating oil tank, or purchased office
supplies during the last 8 years, l imagine that you've noticed it puts a different dent in your wallet today than it
did in 2017. Now imagine having the pleasure of purchasing those things for 100 teenagers and picture the dent MSSM is feeling in our operating budget!
ln June 2024, MSSM submitted a budget proposal for the next biennial (included in this packet) to the Department of Education as requested. We suggested modest increases of $250,000 for the 2025-26 year and
$116,000 for the 2026-27 year. Each year represented about a 3% increase with an additional $140,000 in
year one to support our investment in the School's admission office. Those requests did not add significant spending, did not advance exciting and important new initiatives, and barely provided salary increases in line with inflation. They did not add the additional funding needed to truly meet the financial aid needs of qualified students. Unfortunately, the Department of Education informed the School that they had determined they were
unable to provide any additional funding to MSSM for the next biennial and our budgeted amount remains flat
for the next two years.
With this information, MSSM tightened our belts for yet another budget cycle. The School's administration and
dedicated Board of Trustees identified more non-payroll savings and cut more positions to draft a balanced 2025-26 budget that was approved at the Board's March quarterly meeting (attached to this packet). As that
budget shows, we decreased our FTEs by 2.25 - following a reduction of 3.5 FTEs the year prior. We modeled
a very modest salary increase, falling below the rate of inflation reflected in the CPI for another year. While we continue to focus our limited resources on our student experience, this budget does reduce the number of
classes we will be able to offer next year. We are deferring some maintenance needs for another year. We are
not advancing some of our STEM outreach initiatives The operating funds of $400,000 requested in LD787 will allow us to meet the model we originally planned and presented to the Department of Education, address the deteriorating chimney on our dorm before it fails, and potentially even address some of the initiatives we are
considering as part of our strategic planning process.

ln addition to the operating funds, l urge you to consider ensuring access to MSSM for Maine families by
appropriating the additional $250,000 requested in LD787 for financial aid. As we grow our enrollment numbers
(see attached reports on our admission pipeline this year which is significantly higher than any of the past 5
years) and seek to serve a broader range of the State, we have seen significantly more families qualify for
financial assistance toward the room and board fees. We do not receive additional funding for this aid - and our
current budget for 2025-26 increases the financial aid allotment by $70,000 to a total of $350,000; almost 10% of our entire existing allocation. Even with us setting aside that 10%, we are unable to meet the aid of some
families that qualify through our third party vendor. Those families are faced with undue hardship trying to find
the funding or, worse, have to make the decision not to send their qualified student to the State's STEM
magnet school. The additional funding in LD787 would allow us to redistribute the additional $70,000 back toward operating costs and meet the full need of all families that are accepted and qualify.
Thank you for your time today and for your service to the State of Maine. l look forward to welcoming you to
our campus in Limestone someday and I'm happy to answer any questions the Committee may have.

10040172:
A parent's perspective on the value of our son's education at MSSM
We recognized early that our youngest child was intellectually curious and a quick learner. He was several years younger than his siblings through whom he was exposed to schoolwork and ideas ahead of his own grade level work. In effect, he became comfortable becoming an independent learner.
Lucky for us, at the same time, Jay was a helpful and entertaining younger sibling and a valuable, collaborative member of our household. We proudly admit to being a family that enjoyed discussing topics in science, history, current events, and culture and incorporated these into hands-on learning opportunities and travel.
Jay became aware of MSSM by noticing the flyers for summer camps posted at his school. He attended three summer camps and decided on his own to initiate the paperwork for admission for 9th grade. When we explained that he would need to take standardized tests, he countered that he had already done the search to locate the date and time most convenient for us! Impressed by the proactive and intentional efforts of our 8th grader, we used this opportunity to discuss the cautionary tales of trying and not always achieving. He was certainly ready to take on the challenges of being an MSSM student and we could not pose a barrier to such a clear demonstration of his selfawareness and positive motivation.
Only when Jay got letters of acceptance did we truly realize the tremendous learning opportunities and specialized curriculum he would have at MSSM. The fact that a boarding school offered him an environment where his fellow learners were equally curious and motivated created an immersive experience that Jay thrived on. Being "nerds" and motivated learners was celebrated at MSSM! He was truly among his peers. The smaller class size meant he had more individualized instruction and guidance than what we had experienced at our local school. The highly qualified teachers were able to evaluate Jay's learning style and abilities and were able to become mentors and guides, not merely classroom instructors. Students are also offered the opportunity to mentor younger learners, thus completing the circle of learning and teaching.
I appreciate MSSM's attempt to bring students from diverse backgrounds, including underrepresented groups, to create a broad, thriving learning community. The opportunity to live with people of backgrounds different than his own was unique and valuable to Jay. He became aware of the range of family dynamics, cultures, and personal experiences. This offered both commonalities as well as contrasts to his own world view. Combined with his learning in classes like history, economics, and government, as well as his experiences in clubs at MSSM like Student Senate and Youth In Government, his selection to the United States Senate Youth Program, and a summer spent in Washington, DC as a US Senate Page, I believe Jay became aware of

the role of good public policies in helping to create opportunities for healthy communities and societies. These were invaluable experiences, at a formative time of life, that are inherent to a boarding high school experience like MSSM. I'm not convinced Jay would have had these experiences had he not had teachers, guidance counselors, and caring adults around him who recognized and nurtured both his passions as well as his talents. This boarding school community enabled Jay to become the mature, self-aware, helpful member of society that he manifests today.
Today, as Jay finishes his undergraduate studies (outside our state) he continues to hold Maine in his heart. He has volunteered on a committee studying youth incarceration in Maine and twice has been an electoral college delegate for our great state. He has maintained close ties with many of the friends he made during his four years at MSSM and gathers with them as time allows in their busy young adult lives, either back home in Maine or wherever their paths cross. He certainly has manifested his love and appreciation for what Maine and MSSM have contributed to the opportunities that have revealed themselves to him.
Leigh Philbrick
Sadhana Prasad
Member, MSSM Board of Trustees

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Sue Bernard; I am the State Senator representing District 1, comprised of 37
Communities in Northern Aroostook County.
I am proud to sponsor LD 1011, "An Act to Change the Residency Requirements for State
Funding for Student Tuition at the Maine School of Science and Mathematics."
The other day, when I was preparing for this hearing, I noticed that LD 787 looked very similar to my bill. After discussing with Director Constantine, the Executive Director of the Maine
School of Science and Mathematics in Limestone, I am asking this committee to consider a
sponsor amendment for the work session.
During our discussion, Director Constantine noted a need for clarification in the law goveming
sending districts and secondary schools. The current law mentions MS SM, but it does not discuss what the sending districts are responsible for in compensating MS SM. Sending districts are those
that do not have their own secondary school and send their students to another school or district.
The lack of clarity has led to differences in how sending districts compensate MSSM. This
amendment will specify that districts are responsible for the cost of attendance for these students
and defines this as "The maximum allowable cost of attendance charge at the Maine School of
Science and Mathematics is the actual room and board rate determined by the Maine School of Science and Mathematics Board of Trustees or the state average per public secondary student
cost as adjusted, Whichever is lower."
Director Constantine is here today to testify and will explain a little more of the specifics of this amendment.
